0: On 13 August 2026 DeepSeek open-sourced its first agent product: DeepSeek Harness.
1: The stars grew absurdly fast. I remember it reaching 64.2k stars in a single day, and by the time I wrote this it was at 221K. In one month it gained 220,000 stars. Terrifying.

40: You can enter a DeepSeek API key right away or click “configure later”. If the environment or Harness settings already hold a recognisable key, you may not need to fill it in again; go by the actual page in the current version.

43: Click “Add workspace” on the left and choose a folder you are ready to hand to the Harness. I used an empty test directory, DeepSeek-harness-Work.

46: Mode: Standard, PTC, Minimal or Creative;
48: Model and reasoning level: in my case DeepSeek-V4-Flash High.
49: The first time, never pick an important project straight away. Use an empty directory to confirm permissions and behaviour before touching a real repository.

65: The local “Settings → Agent presets” page shows four preset cards directly, each of which can be viewed or copied, and the page also has an entry to “create a custom preset with Creative mode”.
67: A full coding agent with file editing, Shell, file and web search, Skills, planning, goals, sub-agents and workflows. For a first go, pick this one.
69: It has everything Standard has, and additionally exposes tools through the Code Mode SDK so the model composes multi-step operations in TypeScript programs. Good for batch processing and automation.
71: It keeps only persistent Bash and str_replace_editor, good for minimal environments and model benchmarking.
73: It adds runtime inspection, plugin experiments and custom preset creation on top of Standard, good for heavily modifying the Harness and developing new agent templates.
75: In one sentence: DeepSeek Harness is not just a fixed coding agent, it is more like a “dress-up system that installs abilities into an agent”.
76: The official line: everything is a plugin.
77: Models, tools, skills, sessions, sandboxes, storage, the loop, scheduling and the UI are all plugins. You can swap models, install external tools, hook up Skills, adjust permissions, turn on search, change the interface, call sub-agents, and even recompose the run mode.
78: That sounds like marketing copy, but on my machine, under “Settings → Plugins → Plugin list”, there is a huge list: models, sessions, credentials, sandboxes, permissions, Skills, goals, sub-agents, workflows, web search, workspaces, Trajectory and a pile of UI components.
79: It also provides an append-only session log that puts the system prompt, tool calls, sub-agent scheduling and context injection into one event stream, convenient for recovery, forking, searching and replay.
80: So it is more an agent base developers can keep modifying than simply a “DeepSeek version of Codex”.

95: @stevibe used the Harness to generate a 3D Rubik's cube: 27 minutes, 52 steps. He also stresses that you can inspect every assistant and tool call one by one on the Trajectory page.
96: This case shows that the Harness is not just a tool for changing a few lines of code. Complex tasks needing a long execution chain while keeping full evidence are where it belongs.
98: @NFT_Chen showed a 3D interactive simulation of a four-stroke diesel engine: cylinders, pistons, crankshaft, valve train, fuel, lubrication and cooling systems are all there, and you can drag the view and watch phase and live operating parameters.
99: Compared with “build me a web page”, a task with clear structure, physical logic and interaction requirements shows much better whether the model, tool calling and long-task scheduling really work.
101: @dotey showed a plugin-based UI: the agent conversation and execution on the left, and Explorer, Tasks, a web page or a slides preview opening directly on the right.
102: This may currently be the most mainstream way to show “everything is a plugin”: without touching the agent's core task and only replacing the interaction layer, the Harness becomes a slides workbench, a web workbench or a code previewer.
104: @yanhua1010 made a Harness tutorial on “implementing an AI agent from scratch”, covering the principles, source-code walkthrough, progressive demos and a runnable project.
105: Many people are no longer satisfied with “just installing it”; they want to understand how plugins, the Agent Loop, context and the runtime actually fit together.

109: The installer finally exited with code 0, and dsh plugin --profile web list --depth 0 clearly listed dsh-better-sidebar 0.10.3. On restart I hit that Node version pitfall again: the login shell outside the sandbox defaults to Node.js 22.14.0, while the current DSH persistence module needs a newer Zstd API; after explicitly switching back to the local Node.js 22.19.0, DSH listened normally on 127.0.0.1:39201.
110: Reopening the earlier test session, an Explorer had appeared on the right, showing project-notes.md, tasks.csv and the README.md the Harness generated. The point of this step is that the plugin UI really loaded, not merely that a dependency was written into package.json.
111: Then clicking README.md in the Explorer shows a Markdown preview on the right without leaving the session, and you can switch to editing and save. That is the practical part of the Harness: the agent keeps working on the left while you check files and output on the right. The plugin is not a separate toy; it is assembled into the workbench inside the same runtime.
112: Test conclusion: fully working. Installation, configuration registration, Node compatibility handling, plugin loading, workspace file browsing and live Markdown preview — all six steps verified.
115: The installer exited with code 0, and after restart Creative mode did have the two tools openpencil_new and openpencil_render. I asked it to create an editable 1200×675 harness-case-board.op and explicitly forbade faking it with plain text or SVG.
116: The result: the tool really executed down to the transaction layer and returned OpenPencil editor host binary is unavailable🤔
117: Digging around: there is no OpenPencil.app in /Applications, no corresponding executable on PATH either, and the plugin cache has only render-access.key, with no editor host binary. After the creation failed no .op file remained, so later rendering naturally reported .op file not found.
118: Test conclusion: partly successful. Plugin installation and tool registration are fine, but creating and rendering the editable file did not work. What is missing is not an API key but OpenPencil's desktop/editor host. Installing only the DSH plugin package does not mean you own the external desktop runtime. If you hit the same error, do not fake success by renaming an SVG.
121: Creative mode must temporarily register a task_csv_summary tool in the current session, call it immediately to analyse tasks.csv, and then generate tasks-dashboard.md.
122: The agent first used cordis_inspect_* to query harness.defineTool/registerTool, the Host fs service and the tool list, then used cordis_define to create csvsum-1/pkg-1 and cordis_run to start it as run-1. Tool.listTools confirmed task_csv_summary had entered the current agent's tool set.
123: The key step is not that “the code was written” but that the model's next step really called task_csv_summary("tasks.csv"). The tool read the CSV through the Host fs service and returned: total tasks 3; P0=2, P1=1; pending=2, in progress=1; 2 unfinished P0 items. None of that counting used Bash, Python, a Node script or the model's mental arithmetic — the tool it had just built did the work.
124: The agent then wrote tasks-dashboard.md purely from the JSON the tool returned, and the sidebar opened the Markdown preview immediately. I checked tasks.csv, README.md and project-notes.md byte by byte: not a character had changed.
125: Test conclusion: fully working, and this case shows the Harness difference best.
126: In one session it ran “inspect the runtime → create a plugin → load the plugin → the dynamic tool enters the model's tool set → actually call it → generate a previewable artefact”, all without a restart. Seeing it use the tool it had just built was, I admit, a little stunning. This temporary plugin expires after a restart; to keep it long term, package it as a formal DSH plugin.
128: To open it as fast as possible:
130: When it will not open, first confirm that the Node.js actually running dsh satisfies ^22.19.0 || >=24.0.0; both of my pitfalls were this.
131: Once open: add an API key, choose a test workspace and run a minimal task with Standard mode that can read a file and generate a README. In five minutes you can verify whether it works on your machine.
132: From installing with one command, to a plugin workbench, to the agent building itself a tool while running, DeepSeek Harness is not a “DeepSeek version of Codex”: it splits models, tools and UI into replaceable plugins.It is not a fixed product; you can reassemble it into an agent base of your own along your workflow.
